draft.title: Heuristics in decisions
card: A heuristic is a mental shortcut. It lets us make a decision quickly without weighing up all the information.
judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid or recent events feel more common than they really are.
relying too heavily on the first piece of information we meet, such as a starting price. Later judgements stay close to it.
Heuristics are often good enough and save effort. They can also cause systematic errors, which are mistakes that lean the same way again and again.
draft.remember: Heuristics trade accuracy for speed, so they can lead to the same kinds of mistakes.

a.q: After seeing news reports of shark attacks, Jin decides swimming at the beach is very risky, although attacks are rare. Which heuristic best explains this?
opts: Availability, as vivid examples come to mind easily
Anchoring, as the first piece of information is relied on
Availability, as rare events are weighed up carefully
Anchoring, as the decision comes from a set of beliefs
a.why: Jin judges the risk by how easily shark attacks come to mind after vivid news stories. That is availability. Anchoring is the tempting option, but nothing here is a first piece of information that later judgements stay close to.
a.clue: Think about which examples come to mind easily.

b.q: Priya sees a jacket first marked at $400, then reduced to $200. She thinks it is a bargain and buys it, though similar jackets sell for $150. Which statement best explains her decision?
opts: Her judgement stayed close to the first price she saw
She recalled many examples of jackets that were cheap
She checked the prices of all similar jackets in detail
She judged the jacket by how recent sales had felt
b.why: The $400 price acted as an anchor, so $200 seemed low. This is a systematic error because she did not compare it with other jackets. Availability is tempting because of the sale, but it depends on examples coming to mind, not on a starting price.
b.clue: Which piece of information did Priya meet first?

a.best: Availability, as vivid examples come to mind easily

b.best: Her judgement stayed close to the first price she saw

problems.detail: Why (b) says this is a systematic error 'because she did not compare it with other jackets'. The card defines a systematic error as mistakes that lean the same way again and again, not as failing to compare. This misstates the card's idea, and one purchase is not shown to be a repeated bias.
The clue 'Think about which examples come to mind easily' repeats the wording of the right option and the card's definition of availability. A student can match the words without knowing the idea.
